# Results {#sec-results}

## Model Performance

To answer the research question of whether the bioelectrical plant signal
predicts the participant's emotional state, three machine learning model
architectures are compared (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network), each
of them tested on two feature representations (raw, session-normalized),
resulting in six combinations for each of the three target variables:
valence, arousal, and the proxy emotion label.

Data recording resulted in a dataset including 284 windows from 15
participants. The evaluation was performed using a nested five-fold
cross-validation procedure grouped by participants, ensuring that no
participant appeared in both the training and test data simultaneously
and that the hyperparameter tuning never utilized information from the
test data used to evaluate how well the model performs. This ensures
that the reported values are reliable and avoids leakage. For statistical
validation, a permutation test with 200 label permutations was
additionally performed to assess how likely the obtained result would be
under the null hypothesis that the plant features carry no information
about the label.

### Valence Classification

The target variable valence, determined by FER (HSEmotion), contains
three classes: negative, neutral, and positive. Across the six
combinations, accuracy ranges from 36% to 43%. @fig-valence
represents all six combinations sorted by their macro-F1 value.

![Classifier comparison for the target variable valence.](figures/valence_comparison.png){#fig-valence width=80%}

![Confusion matrices for the target variable valence: pooled over the five outer folds of the nested cross-validation, for all six (model, representation) combinations. Rows hold the proxy label and columns the model's prediction, so the diagonal counts the correctly classified windows and each panel sums to the 284 windows of the dataset.](figures/confusion_valence.png){#fig-cm-valence width=95%}

Of the six (model, representation) combinations compared, Random Forest on
the session-normalized features performed the best, with an accuracy of
43% and a macro-F1 of 0.42. The permutation test confirms that this result
is statistically significant (p = 0.005; @fig-perm-valence). Zero out of
200 random label permutations matched or exceeded the result actually
observed.
Therefore, valence is the target variable for which the plant signal
shows the clearest and most robustly validated predictability. In
addition, all three classes of valence were recognized with similar
accuracy: this combination predicted negative, neutral, and positive with
per-class F1 scores of 0.43, 0.45, and 0.40 respectively (@fig-cm-valence). In contrast to
the emotion classification, there was no significant bias toward a
dominant class in this case. Averaged across all three models, the effect
of session normalization increases the macro-F1 scores by 0.031 for this
target variable. For Random Forest, the improvement compared to the raw
representation of 0.068 is the highest and highlights the strongest
individual case across all target variables.

| Target   | Best model                          | Accuracy | Macro-F1 |    p    |
|----------|--------------------------------------|:--------:|:--------:|:-------:|
| Valence  | Random Forest (session-normalized)   |   43%    |   0.42   |  0.005  |
| Arousal  | Neural Network (session-normalized)  |   37%    |   0.36   |  0.055  |
| Emotion  | Random Forest (raw)                  |   42%    |   0.21   |  0.015  |

: Model performance by target variable: best (model, representation) combination per target, with its pooled nested cross-validation scores and its permutation-test p-value. {#tbl-perf}

@tbl-perf summarizes the best combination per target variable.

The plant voltage carries a session-dependent baseline that has nothing
to do with the participant's emotions, so which features the winning
model leans on is itself informative. Its two highest-ranked predictors are the
Hjorth dynamics descriptors `hjorth_mobility` (how quickly the signal
changes) and `hjorth_complexity` (how that rate of change itself varies),
followed by `plant_min` and `plant_range`. The dynamics descriptors are
level-invariant by construction, and the amplitude descriptors behind them
enter only in their session-normalized form, so they express how far a
window departs from that session's own baseline rather than where the
session sits in absolute terms. The model therefore relies mainly on how
the curve moves within the window, not on where it lies overall. This is
an indication that the model is learning about the actual signal dynamics
and not recognizing a session based on its random baseline. Feature
rankings throughout this chapter are read off the tree-based models tuned
on the full dataset, which is the only place the pipeline exposes them;
they are diagnostic and are not themselves a reported performance metric.

### Arousal Classification

The target variable arousal, derived from HRV (RMSSD) and the mean heart
rate, contains three classes: calm, neutral, and activated. None of the
classifiers are able to predict arousal better than random: across the six
combinations, accuracy ranges from 32% to 37%, which is close to the
approximately 33% expected by chance with three classes (see @fig-arousal).

![Classifier comparison for the target variable arousal.](figures/arousal_comparison.png){#fig-arousal width=80%}

![Confusion matrices for the target variable arousal: pooled over the five outer folds of the nested cross-validation, for all six (model, representation) combinations. Rows hold the proxy label and columns the model's prediction, so the diagonal counts the correctly classified windows and each panel sums to the 284 windows of the dataset.](figures/confusion_arousal.png){#fig-cm-arousal width=95%}

Nevertheless, the Neural Network on the session-normalized features
performed the best, at an accuracy of 37% and a macro-F1 of 0.36. The
result does not quite reach the threshold to be statistically significant
(p = 0.055; 10 of 200 permutations matched or exceeded it;
@fig-perm-arousal). The
classification report shows that this combination classified all three
classes with similarly low accuracy, at per-class F1 scores of 0.35
(activated), 0.30 (calm), and 0.42 (neutral), so no class is recognized
appreciably better than the others (@fig-cm-arousal). However, it must be
noted that there is an unbalanced distribution of the classes: "neutral"
is clearly the largest class, with 115 out of 284 cases (approximately
40.5%), while
80 cases are labeled activated, and 89 calm. The approach of session
normalization is most effective and consistent for the target variable
arousal, improving the macro-F1 scores of all three models, by an average
of 0.035. As with valence, DC-invariant and session-relative features
dominate the ranking. Because the winning multilayer perceptron exposes no
feature importances, the ranking is read from the tree-based models on the
same session-normalized representation; it is led by `spike_rate` (the
frequency of transient amplitude fluctuations), `plant_max`, and
`bp_15_30`, with `spectral_entropy` (spectral disorder) following.

### Emotion Classification

Regarding our research question, our most important target variable is
emotion. Similar to the Circumplex Model [@russell1980], our emotion
label is created by combining the valence and arousal results, leading to
five classes: negative activated, negative calm, neutral, positive
activated, positive calm. The best-performing combination is
Random Forest on the raw representation, with an accuracy of 42% and a
macro-F1 score of 0.21 (see @fig-emotion).

![Classifier comparison for the target variable emotion.](figures/emotion_comparison.png){#fig-emotion width=80%}

![Confusion matrices for the target variable emotion: pooled over the five outer folds of the nested cross-validation, for all six (model, representation) combinations. Rows hold the proxy label and columns the model's prediction, so the diagonal counts the correctly classified windows and each panel sums to the 284 windows of the dataset.](figures/confusion_emotion.png){#fig-cm-emotion width=95%}

This is the only case where the raw representation performs better than
the session-normalized one, contradicting the otherwise consistent
trend. Regarding the target variable emotion, there is a significant
class imbalance, as "neutral" dominates: 177 of the 284 windows carry it,
and it is the only class the winning model recognizes reliably (F1 0.64).
This is the reason why the accuracy of 42% appears so much
higher than the macro-F1 score of 0.21. The model largely
predicts the majority class well while barely distinguishing the
minority classes (F1 0.08 for "positive activated", 0.07 for "negative
calm"), as reflected in the much lower macro-F1 of 0.211 (@fig-cm-emotion). So while emotion
prediction is statistically better than a random classifier, accuracy
alone overstates how much the model actually understands about emotional
states. The permutation test verified the statistical significance
(p = 0.015; @fig-perm-emotion), but it is weaker than for valence. The feature ranking for
this target is led by `plant_max`, `ratio_bp1_5_bp5_15`, and
`plant_median`, that is by amplitude and spectral-shape descriptors, with
the Hjorth dynamics descriptors following. This is a different profile
from the other two targets, and one to be read with the caveat that this model
largely reproduces the majority class.

## Correlation Analysis

H2 is tested on valence, the target for which the plant signal predicts
above chance.

![Confounding triangle and partial correlations: the plant, valence and CO~2~ triangle, and the per-feature partial correlation with valence before and after removing CO~2~.](figures/co2_correlation.jpeg){#fig-co2 width=95%}

@fig-co2 summarizes the confounding triangle and the per-feature partial
correlation results discussed below.

The correlation analysis is conducted in two complementary variants. In
the raw analysis, plant features showed a weak but frequently
significant correlation with valence (mean $|\rho|$ = 0.140, significant
in 13 of 22 features), while the correlation between plant features and
CO~2~ concentration, evaluated at its optimal time lag (a change in
ambient CO~2~ is expected to affect the plant voltage only after a short
delay), was substantially stronger (mean $|\rho|$ = 0.420, significant in
18 of 22 features). CO~2~ itself was also correlated with valence
($\rho$ = 0.308, p \< 0.0001). Together, these three pairwise
relationships form a plausible confounding triangle: CO~2~ correlates
with both the plant signal and valence, raising the question of whether
the plant--valence relationship is genuine or merely an artifact of CO~2~
acting on both variables independently. To test this directly, we
computed the partial correlation between plant features and valence
while controlling for CO~2~. If CO~2~ were the true driver of the
plant--valence association, this partial correlation should collapse
toward zero. Instead it barely moved: the mean $|\rho|$ went from 0.140 to
0.145, a change of roughly three percent and in the direction opposite to
the one a confound would produce, with the same 13 of 22 features
remaining significant. Controlling for CO~2~ therefore removes none of the
plant--valence association.

The session-normalized analysis provided further insight into the nature
of the CO~2~ effect. Once between-session variance (e.g., differences in
room climate across recording days) was removed, the plant--CO~2~
correlation (at optimal lag) dropped sharply to a mean $|\rho|$ of 0.101,
significant in only 4 of 22 features, and was no longer
classified as a robust, present effect. This indicates that most of the
raw plant--CO~2~ coupling reflects slow, session-level environmental
drift rather than a genuine within-session physiological interaction.
Despite this reduction, the plant--valence partial correlation remained
stable under CO~2~ control within sessions as well (mean $|\rho|$ 0.075 to
0.074, a change of roughly one percent), confirming the
confound-rejection result at both the between- and within-session level.
